prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "BRISTOL MYERS SQUIBB CO" (ticker BMY), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "BMY", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Bristol-Myers Squibb Company
markets: Hematology (multiple myeloma, anemia, lymphoma, CAR-T cell therapy)
Immunology (rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, ulcerative colitis, multiple sclerosis)

mission.statement: our mission is to discover, develop and deliver innovative medicines that help patients prevail over serious diseases.
mission.source: 'About Bristol Myers Squibb' section of the company's Q2 2026 earnings release (July 30, 2026); its 2025 proxy statement also states the vision 'to transform patients' lives through science'
mission.plain: Invent and sell medicines that help people beat serious illnesses like cancer, blood clots and heart disease.

about.plain: Bristol Myers Squibb invents and sells prescription medicines. Its biggest seller is Eliquis, a pill that stops dangerous blood clots, and Opdivo, a drug that helps the body's immune system fight cancer. It also makes medicines for blood cancers, heart disease and schizophrenia. Scientists there spend billions of dollars every year trying to find the next medicines before old ones lose patent protection and get cheap copies.
about.customers: Doctors prescribe its medicines to patients, and they are bought by wholesalers, pharmacies, hospitals and paid for largely by insurers and governments such as Medicare.
about.everyday: Eliquis, the blood thinner advertised on TV and taken by millions of people with atrial fibrillation, is its best-selling product.

money.plain: pill that prevents strokes and blood clots, sold with Pfizer
multiple myeloma pills now losing sales to generics

money.part: Newer blood medicines and cell therapy
money.plain: Reblozyl for anemia, Breyanzi and Abecma CAR-T
new kind of schizophrenia pill, also tested in Alzheimer's psychosis

result.summary: BMS has a real but temporary moat built on patents and specialist know-how: Eliquis ($14,443M in 2025) and Opdivo ($10,049M) are protected in the US until about 2028, and it has strong positions in hematology and cell therapy. The moat is being tested by heavy patent expiries (Revlimid sales fell 49% in 2025), Medicare price negotiation and Keytruda's lead in PD-1 drugs, so its advantage depends on newer drugs such as Reblozyl, Breyanzi, Camzyos and Cobenfy, which made its Growth Portfolio $26,409M (up 17%) in 2025.

pricingPower.evidence: Patented drugs command high prices (Eliquis sales rose 8% in 2025 and 22% in Q2 2026), but Medicare's negotiated 'maximum fair price' for Eliquis took effect on January 1, 2026 and for Pomalyst from January 1, 2027, and generics cut Revlimid sales from $5,773M (2024) to $2,951M (2025).

moats.evidence: Patents protect its key drugs, but exclusivity is time-limited: BMS estimates US exclusivity for Eliquis and Opdivo until 2028, Eliquis EU patents expire in November 2026, and Revlimid and Pomalyst already face generics.
Patients stable on Eliquis or on long-term therapies such as Orencia and Reblozyl are rarely switched, but insurers and formularies can force moves to cheaper alternatives once generics arrive.
A medicine does not become more valuable to a patient because others use it.
It spent $9,951M on R&D in 2025 and runs a global sales force, scale that small rivals cannot match, though giants such as Merck, Roche and J&J are as large or larger.
Some niches such as CAR-T cell therapy and cardiac myosin inhibitors support only a few players, but most of its markets have several large competitors.
BMS uses the same patent-and-sales-force model as other big pharma companies, so rivals face no conflict in copying it.
Manufacturing personalised CAR-T therapies (Breyanzi sales up 82% to $1,358M in 2025) and radiopharmaceuticals from its RayzeBio deal require specialised know-how that few rivals have.

Exclusive rights to first-in-class medicines such as Camzyos and Cobenfy (a muscarinic schizophrenia drug) and to new drugs like iberdomide (Zenbexus, accelerated approval in August 2026) are cornered assets while patents last.

customers.evidence: Doctors keep prescribing Eliquis, the leading anticoagulant (worldwide sales $14,443M in 2025, up 8%), but Opdivo's share of combined Opdivo and Keytruda sales fell from 32.7% in 2020 to 24.5% in 2025, showing oncologists prefer Merck's drug.

talent.evidence: BMS was named one of Great Place to Work's World's Best Workplaces in 2022 and its Italian unit ranked second in its category on Best Workplaces Italia 2026, but it is not a fixture of the top US employer rankings and cut SG&A by 11% in 2025 under its productivity initiative.

product.evidence: Several products lead their classes (Eliquis in anticoagulants, Camzyos as the first cardiac myosin inhibitor, Cobenfy as a new schizophrenia mechanism), but Opdivo trails Keytruda, Cobenfy sales were only $155M in 2025, and the Phase 3 Librexia ACS trial of milvexian was stopped in November 2025.

competitors.name: Merck & Co.
competitors.note: Keytruda (and subcutaneous Keytruda Qlex) is the leading PD-1 drug against Opdivo and Opdivo Qvantig across lung, melanoma and other cancers.

competitors.name: Johnson & Johnson
competitors.note: Xarelto versus Eliquis in anticoagulation (US); Darzalex, Carvykti and Tecvayli versus Revlimid, Pomalyst, Abecma and iberdomide in multiple myeloma; Caplyta versus Cobenfy in schizophrenia; partner on milvexian.

competitors.name: Roche
competitors.note: Tecentriq PD-L1 drug against Opdivo and Columvi/Lunsumio bispecifics in lymphoma versus Breyanzi; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: AstraZeneca
competitors.note: Imfinzi versus Opdivo in lung and other cancers, and a broad oncology portfolio competing for the same patients.

competitors.name: Bayer
competitors.note: Markets Xarelto outside the US against Eliquis; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Pfizer
competitors.note: Co-markets Eliquis with BMS but competes in oncology (Padcev, Lorbrena) and immunology (Velsipity versus Zeposia).

competitors.name: Gilead Sciences (Kite)
competitors.note: Yescarta and Tecartus CAR-T therapies compete with Breyanzi, and its anito-cel (with Arcellx) targets multiple myeloma against Abecma.

competitors.name: AbbVie
competitors.note: Vraylar versus Cobenfy in schizophrenia, Rinvoq and Skyrizi versus Zeposia and Sotyktu, and Venclexta in blood cancers.

competitors.name: Novartis
competitors.note: Kymriah CAR-T and radioligand therapies (Lutathera, Pluvicto) competing with Breyanzi and RayzeBio's RYZ101.

competitors.name: Amgen
competitors.note: Otezla versus Sotyktu in psoriasis and Kyprolis in multiple myeloma.

competitors.name: Cytokinetics
competitors.note: Aficamten, a cardiac myosin inhibitor, challenges Camzyos in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

competitors.name: Regeneron
competitors.note: Libtayo PD-1 drug and Lynozyfic bispecific in multiple myeloma.

competitors.name: Daiichi Sankyo
competitors.note: Edoxaban (Lixiana/Savaysa) anticoagulant competing with Eliquis, mainly outside the US; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Generic drug makers (Teva, Viatris, Dr. Reddy's and others)
competitors.note: Generic lenalidomide and pomalidomide are eroding Revlimid and Pomalyst, and generic apixaban is expected in the US from 2028.

estimates.name: Generic drug makers (Teva, Viatris, Dr. Reddy's and others)

marketShare.measure: share of combined worldwide sales of the two leading PD-1 drugs (company-reported: Opdivo incl. Qvantig $10,287M vs Keytruda incl. Qlex $31,680M in 2025; $6,992M vs $14,380M in 2020); excludes other PD-1/PD-L1 drugs

threats: Patent cliff: BMS estimates US exclusivity for Eliquis ($14,443M in 2025) and Opdivo ($10,049M) ends around 2028, Eliquis EU patents expire in November 2026, and Revlimid and Pomalyst are already losing sales to generics.
US drug-price controls: Medicare's negotiated price for Eliquis took effect in January 2026 and for Pomalyst takes effect in January 2027, with more drugs likely to be selected.
Competition from Merck's Keytruda and subcutaneous Keytruda Qlex in PD-1, J&J and others in multiple myeloma, and Cytokinetics' aficamten against Camzyos.
Pipeline risk: the Phase 3 Librexia ACS trial of milvexian was stopped in November 2025, and growth depends on new launches such as Cobenfy ($155M in 2025) succeeding.
Heavy debt from acquisitions (Karuna, RayzeBio, Mirati): $43,120M of debt against $11,464M of cash and marketable securities at June 30, 2026.

ceo.name: Christopher Boerner
ceo.background: PhD and MA in business administration from UC Berkeley's Haas School and BA from Washington University in St. Louis; former McKinsey consultant, Genentech marketing leader and Seattle Genetics executive who joined BMS in 2015, ran commercial operations and became CEO in November 2023 and Board Chair in April 2024.

c1.evidence: BMS is a large established drugmaker in a mature industry; its 2025 revenue of $48,194M was flat versus 2024 and below leaders such as Merck and J&J.

c2.evidence: Doctors choose its drugs for proven clinical benefit (Eliquis, Opdivo, Reblozyl, Camzyos), but the advantage rests on patents that run out, with US exclusivity for Eliquis and Opdivo expected to end around 2028.

c3.evidence: Eliquis is widely known from TV advertising, but the Bristol Myers Squibb name itself is less familiar to ordinary people and it is not the default leader in oncology, where Keytruda leads.

c4.evidence: It repeats its vision 'to transform patients' lives through science' and the mission of helping patients 'prevail over serious diseases', but recent strategy has been dominated by cost cuts and replacing lost patent revenue.

c6.evidence: “big pharma, Eliquis, cancer drugs”: the impression is mostly neutral to positive about its medicines, tempered by general public distrust of drug pricing.

c7.evidence: Its markets (cancer, cardiovascular disease, neuroscience) are large and growing with ageing populations, but BMS is not riding a secular trend in the way NVDA or CRWD are, and its own sales are flat.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into neuroscience (Cobenfy, including Alzheimer's psychosis trials), radiopharmaceuticals (RayzeBio's RYZ101 met its Phase 3 interim endpoint in October 2026) and new myeloma drugs, though these are still small.

m1.evidence: Boerner has set out a plan to rebuild growth through a 'Growth Portfolio' and new modalities like cell therapy and radiopharmaceuticals, but his focus has been on execution and cost discipline rather than a sweeping vision.

m2.evidence: Boerner is a hired executive who joined BMS in 2015 and became CEO in November 2023, not a founder.

m4.evidence: There is no clear public evidence either way about a servant-leadership style under Boerner.

m5.evidence: BMS has a strong scientific culture, but much of its recent innovation was bought (Celgene 2019, MyoKardia, Karuna, RayzeBio, Mirati) rather than invented internally.

m6.evidence: Boerner's background is in business and commercial strategy (PhD in business administration, McKinsey, marketing roles), not science or engineering.

m7.evidence: Under Boerner BMS emphasises patient impact and access programmes, but there is no distinctive public record of him championing causes beyond the business.

m7b.evidence: There is no record of Boerner giving a commencement speech at a top university; he gave a keynote at the MIT Sloan healthcare conference in 2025, which is not a commencement address.

m8b.evidence: Boerner keeps a low-key, executive profile typical of big-pharma CEOs.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO the Growth Portfolio rose 17% to $26,409M in 2025 and 2026 guidance was raised to $49.0-50.0B of revenue in July 2026, but 2024 brought a $8,948M net loss from acquired IPRD charges and milvexian's ACS trial was stopped.

m10.evidence: BMS runs a strategic productivity initiative that cut non-GAAP SG&A by 11% to $7.1B in 2025, but it is not known for Bezos-style frugality.

c10.evidence: Its medicines help millions of patients worldwide (Eliquis prevents strokes, Opdivo extends survival in many cancers), though they treat specific diseases rather than serving billions of people every day.

p2.evidence: Discovering and getting approval for new medicines such as CAR-T cell therapies and first-in-class drugs like Camzyos and Cobenfy is very hard and important to patients.

f2.evidence: Gross margin (excluding amortisation) slipped from 72.3% in 2020 to 71.1% in 2025, while operating margin swung from -21.6% to 20.8% because of large acquired IPRD charges in 2020 and 2024.

f3.evidence: Shareholders' equity is positive ($18,473M at end-2025), but debt of $43,120M at June 30, 2026 far exceeds cash and marketable securities of $11,464M and is about 3 times 2025 operating cash flow of $14,156M.

f4.evidence: Operating income (revenue less operating expenses) rose from -$9,185M in 2020 to $10,002M in 2025, but operating cash flow was flat ($14,052M in 2020 vs $14,156M in 2025) and below 2021's $16,207M.

v1.evidence: Eliquis is widely seen as the leading oral anticoagulant, but Opdivo is second to Keytruda, which took 75.5% of their combined 2025 sales.

v2.evidence: BMS was on Great Place to Work's World's Best Workplaces list in 2022 and appears on several national lists (e.g. second in its category in Best Workplaces Italia 2026), but it is not a regular in the top US employer rankings.

c5.evidence: Patients with atrial fibrillation, cancers such as melanoma and lung cancer, multiple myeloma and schizophrenia would miss its medicines, though generic and rival drugs could replace some of them.
